description: Hi! I am Rory. I am the Counter-Factual Ember Calendar (CFEC) team! I am a 5th year student at Queen's University doing a dual-degree in physics and CS. I have done dark matter research on the DEAP-3600 collaboration; worked on Acadien genealogy in Nova Scotia; ran tech at Tricode Cloud, a Canadian startup; won Chengdu80, an international FinTech hackathon in China; co-founded the Queen's Astro-Lens Club; volunteered for SEDS-Canada, SEDS-USA, and the Queen's Space Conference; and more.
summary:
Satellites have recorded Earth's fires for 25 years, but NASA's MODIS (since 2000, now retiring) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire differently, so their records don't match. Ember Calendar joins them into one consistent global record.

Data: we combine 10 open datasets, 8 from NASA: fire detections from four satellites, plus burned area, land cover, vegetation, water, terrain and weather. Together they describe fire and help explain it.

Science: we calibrate 490 million detections so both sensors agree, cutting the error from 65% to 2.5% on held-out years. Rekindle, our simulator, uses the Rothermel fire-spread equations to replay real fires, including the Chilecito fire from the challenge video, and is checked against two satellite references.

Tech: no server. Pick any place and your browser shows its fire calendar, fire season, and how now compares with the past, in about a second, with CSV export. In Rekindle, change the wind and watch a real fire spread differently. The code and data are open, so any agency can run it itself.
details:
Project description

Ember Calendar: 25 years of fire, one consistent record

Live app: https://cf-ember-calendar.pages.dev/ (soon also at embercalendar.earth) ·

Code: https://github.com/Incandescent-Turtle/cf-ember-calendar

Satellites have recorded Earth's fires since 2000, but the record is split between two NASA sensors that can't be compared directly. Ember Calendar joins them into one global record and turns it into a fire calendar for any place on Earth. Rekindle, our fire simulator, then replays real fires and asks: what if the wind had been stronger, or the vegetation drier?

The problem

MODIS (on Terra and Aqua, since 2000) is retiring. VIIRS (since 2012) has finer pixels and catches smaller fires, so it records 2.5 to 3.3 times as much activity for the same burning. Splice the two together and every region's history jumps in 2012 for reasons that have nothing to do with fire. As CONAE's Marina Compagnucci says in the challenge video, without a fix "almost 10 years of historical information will be lost."

Emergency teams need to know: is this month unusual here, and when does our fire season start? That needs one consistent record.

The data: 10 datasets, one picture

Each dataset answers a different question. On their own they are separate archives. Together they can describe a fire and explain it.

- FIRMS MODIS active fires, Terra and Aqua (NASA): Where was fire seen, 2000 onward?

- FIRMS VIIRS active fires, Suomi NPP (NASA): Where was fire seen, in finer detail, 2012 onward?

- FIRMS VIIRS active fires, NOAA-20 (NASA): The same, continuing after Suomi NPP stopped (Nov 2026).

- MCD64A1 burned area (NASA): What actually burned?

- MCD12Q1 land cover (NASA): What vegetation was there to burn?

- MOD44B vegetation cover (NASA): Which ground is bare and can't burn?

- MOD44W water mask (NASA): Where are the natural firebreaks?

- MERRA-2 hourly weather (NASA): How strong was the wind, and how dry was the air?

- Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (ESA): How steep is the ground? (Fire runs uphill.)

- Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery (ESA / EOX): What does the place look like? (Map background.)

That is 490 million fire detections from four NASA satellites, plus six layers describing the land and the weather. The hero fire is the one in the challenge video: Chilecito, La Rioja, July 2026.

The science, part 1: making two sensors agree

  1. Clean. Keep vegetation fires only, drop low-confidence detections, remove gas flares and duplicates.
  2. A fair unit. Instead of counting detections, count fire-cell-days: each ~1 km square that had fire on a given day counts once. Extra VIIRS pixels and extra satellite passes no longer inflate the number.
  3. Calibrate. For each region and month, measure how much more VIIRS sees than MODIS during the years both flew (2013–2021), and scale MODIS by that factor. The factor ranges from about 1.7 to 6.7 across the world, so a single global number would be wrong almost everywhere. The app uses the most local factor with enough data.
  4. Test. Hide one year, calibrate on the others, and check how well MODIS alone reproduces VIIRS for the hidden year:

Held-out-year test, 2013–2021 (median monthly error, global):

- Raw counts, no calibration: 75.9 %

- Fire-cell-days, no calibration: 64.9 %

- Fire-cell-days, calibrated (ours): 2.5 %

The jump at the 2012 handover falls from 1.01 to −0.03 (log units, global), and the shape of the fire season before and after 2012 matches (median r = 0.91 across 224 regions). What we can't prove: values before 2012, because VIIRS didn't exist yet. The Methodology page says so.

The science, part 2: Rekindle and the Rothermel model

Rekindle uses the Rothermel (1972) fire-spread equations, the physics inside standard US fire-behaviour tools such as BehavePlus and FARSITE. From the vegetation, the slope, the wind and the fuel moisture, they work out how fast a fire's edge moves. We move that edge across real terrain on a 90 m grid, hour by hour, with real weather, starting from the fire's first satellite detection. The code passes 10 verification tests, including published Rothermel reference values (within 0.12 %).

How it is judged. The harmonized hotspots record when each spot first burned, and NASA's burned-area map records what burned. So every simulation is scored against two satellite references (the second partly independent of the first), using rules written down before the runs.

- Central British Columbia, 2024: The whole fire matches the mapped burn shape. With double the wind it would have burned 2.9× the area; with calm air, about half.

- Chilecito, Argentina, 2026 (the challenge video fire): One 24-hour stretch matched the satellite timing (2.3 h error, within the 3.2 h limit). With double the wind, 60 % more ground burned that day.

- Córdoba, Argentina, 2024: One 24-hour stretch (shape only).

- Northern Saskatchewan, 2023: Whole-fire footprint, labelled exploratory.

We also publish what failed. No fire matched hour-by-hour over its whole life: real fires burst and stall because of firefighting, roads and local winds that no global dataset records. At Chilecito you can see one cause on the map: the 50 km weather model's wind blew the simulated fire north-east, while the real burn went south-west. What-ifs are shown only where the model passed its test, and they are illustrative, not forecasts.

The tech: one interface, no server

  • Anyone can use it. Draw an area, enter a point and radius, search a place, pick a country, or try one of six ready-made examples (the Rekindle fires, Australia's Black Summer, the Amazon burn season).
  • The calendar shows years × months of fire activity, an "above / below normal" view, the fire season, the trend, the most unusual months, and how this month compares with the past. Hover any cell to see the raw MODIS and VIIRS numbers behind it.
  • Fast without a server. The pipeline turns the full FIRMS archive into 132 MB of compact tiles. Your browser downloads only the tiles it needs and computes everything locally, in about a second for a country. Hosting costs nothing.
  • Runs anywhere, open to all. For the hackathon, the whole global harmonization ran on one 16 GB desktop PC, and the Rekindle simulations ran on a Digital Research Alliance of Canada supercomputer. Neither is required. The code is open source and every input is a free public dataset, so a fire agency, university or research institute can rebuild the record, add its own region, or run its own fires on its own machines.
  • The same answer everywhere. The Python pipeline and the in-browser TypeScript are tested against the same reference files, so the numbers match to the decimal.
  • Rekindle's simulations run ahead of time (on the cluster for the hackathon) and ship as small files, so the what-ifs play instantly.
  • Take it with you. Calendar, hotspots and summary export as CSV / JSON / PNG.
  • Accessible. Colour ramps are tested in code for colour-blind viewers. Every chart has a plain-language caption.

Benefits and impact

  • For early-warning and emergency teams: see in seconds whether this month is unusual for their area, and when the fire season starts.
  • For land managers and scientists: a consistent 25-year baseline for trends and seasonality, with the method published and data exportable to GIS, R or Python.
  • For planners and educators: watch how wind and dryness would have changed a real fire.
  • It keeps the MODIS years usable. As MODIS retires, its 12 years before VIIRS stay comparable with everything after them.
  • Free and global. It works for any place on Earth, needs no account, and costs nothing to host. The code and data are open, so agencies can run and extend it themselves.

The impact we want: anyone responsible for a landscape can check its fire history and spot unusual activity early, from one consistent record. Next steps: daily updates from FIRMS near-real-time feeds, finer fuel maps, and live fire perimeters for Rekindle, toward a tool that could one day support prediction.

What's creative

  • The hotspots become an answer key. The harmonized record gives a "first seen burning" time for every pixel of every fire. We use that to test a physics fire model automatically, anywhere on Earth. Agencies normally tune these models by hand.
  • Two satellites check each other. Rekindle is scored against both the hotspots and NASA's burned-area map. Comparing the two showed how fuzzy each one is on its own.
  • What-ifs are earned, not assumed. A what-if only appears where the model passed a test we wrote down before running it.
  • Calibration that adapts to your area. The app fits the MODIS-to-VIIRS factor to the area you draw, and falls back to a regional or global factor when the area has too little data.

What we considered

  • Honesty over hype. We wrote tests down before running them, published the failures, and never call the what-ifs forecasts.
  • Traceability. Every number in the app shows the raw MODIS and VIIRS values and the calibration factor behind it.
  • Accessibility. Colour ramps are tested in code for colour-blind viewers. The wording is plain and the unit is defined where it appears.
  • Cost and longevity. We chose no server, static files and free hosting, so the tool keeps running after the hackathon.
  • The people who asked. The hero example is the fire from CONAE's challenge video, and the features follow the challenge brief: area selection, the calendar, comparison with the historical median, critical periods and CSV export.
  • Limits of the data. These are listed below and on the Methodology page.

Limitations

Hotspots are not burned area, and clouds or smoke hide some fires. Calibration assumes the MODIS–VIIRS relationship is stable over time. Rekindle models surface fire only (no crown fire, ember spotting or firefighting) with fuels from 500 m land cover and one weather point per fire.

Tools, languages and hardware

  • Languages: Python (data pipeline, Rekindle simulator), TypeScript (web app).
  • Software: DuckDB, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-fmm, rasterio · React, Vite, MapLibre GL, ECharts, Terra Draw · pytest, Vitest.
  • Hardware: a 16 GB desktop PC for the global harmonization build. The Digital Research Alliance of Canada's Fir supercomputer (Slurm) for the fire simulations.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages (app), Hugging Face Datasets (data files).

Use of AI

We used AI coding agents (Claude Code) to write and test code and documentation under our direction. The design, scientific decisions and every reported number were reviewed by the team and come from logged runs.
